import json
import subprocess

def fetch_page(page_id, chunk=0, cursor=None):
    payload = {
        'pageId': page_id,
        'limit': 100,
        'cursor': cursor or {'stack': []},
        'chunkNumber': chunk,
        'verticalColumns': False
    }
    with open('payload.json', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        json.dump(payload, f)
    out_file = f'notion_{page_id}_{chunk}.json'
    subprocess.run([
        'curl.exe', '-s', '-X', 'POST',
        'https://tum-ai.notion.site/api/v3/loadPageChunk',
        '-H', 'Content-Type: application/json',
        '-H', 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)',
        '-d', '@payload.json',
        '-o', out_file
    ], check=True)
    with open(out_file, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        return json.load(f)

with open('notion_out.json', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    res = json.load(f)

blocks = res.get('recordMap', {}).get('block', {})
lines = []
subpages = []

for bid, bdata in blocks.items():
    val = bdata.get('value', {})
    if 'value' in val and 'type' not in val:
        val = val['value']
    btype = val.get('type')
    props = val.get('properties', {})
    title = props.get('title', [])
    parts = []
    for t in title:
        txt = t[0]
        if len(t) > 1:
            for fmt in t[1]:
                if fmt[0] == 'a':
                    txt += f' ({fmt[1]})'
                elif fmt[0] == 'p':
                    txt += f' [page:{fmt[1]}]'
                    subpages.append(fmt[1])
        parts.append(txt)
    text = ''.join(parts)
    lines.append(f'[{btype}] ({bid}): {text}')
    if btype in ['page', 'collection_view', 'collection_view_page', 'external_object_instance', 'bookmark', 'embed', 'file', 'pdf', 'code', 'callout']:
        lines.append(f'   PROPS: {json.dumps(props, ensure_ascii=False)}')
        if btype == 'page' and bid != '3eb7306b-fd62-8089-93e9-ec18c2d64834':
            subpages.append(bid)

with open('notion_parsed.md', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('\n'.join(lines))

print(f'Wrote {len(lines)} lines. Found subpages: {subpages}')
print('Cursor:', res.get('cursor'))

import json
import subprocess

def fetch_page(page_id, chunk=0, cursor=None):
    payload = {
        'pageId': page_id,
        'limit': 100,
        'cursor': cursor or {'stack': []},
        'chunkNumber': chunk,
        'verticalColumns': False
    }
    with open('payload.json', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        json.dump(payload, f)
    out_file = f'notion_{page_id}_{chunk}.json'
    subprocess.run([
        'curl.exe', '-s', '-X', 'POST',
        'https://tum-ai.notion.site/api/v3/loadPageChunk',
        '-H', 'Content-Type: application/json',
        '-H', 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)',
        '-d', '@payload.json',
        '-o', out_file
    ], check=True)
    with open(out_file, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        return json.load(f)

page_id = '3eb7306b-fd62-8089-93e9-ec18c2d64834'
all_blocks = {}
cursor = {'stack': []}
chunk = 0

while True:
    res = fetch_page(page_id, chunk, cursor)
    blocks = res.get('recordMap', {}).get('block', {})
    all_blocks.update(blocks)
    cursor = res.get('cursor', {})
    print(f'Chunk {chunk}: got {len(blocks)} blocks, total {len(all_blocks)}')
    if not cursor.get('stack'):
        break
    chunk += 1
    if chunk > 10:
        break

lines = []
subpages = []

for bid, bdata in all_blocks.items():
    val = bdata.get('value', {})
    if 'value' in val and 'type' not in val:
        val = val['value']
    btype = val.get('type')
    props = val.get('properties', {})
    title = props.get('title', [])
    parts = []
    for t in title:
        txt = t[0]
        if len(t) > 1:
            for fmt in t[1]:
                if fmt[0] == 'a':
                    txt += f' ({fmt[1]})'
                elif fmt[0] == 'p':
                    txt += f' [page:{fmt[1]}]'
                    subpages.append(fmt[1])
        parts.append(txt)
    text = ''.join(parts)
    if btype == 'table_row':
        # extract all cell values in props
        row_cells = []
        for k, v in props.items():
            cell_txt = ''.join([c[0] for c in v]) if isinstance(v, list) else str(v)
            row_cells.append(cell_txt)
        text = ' | '.join(row_cells)
    lines.append(f'[{btype}] ({bid}): {text}')
    if btype in ['page', 'collection_view', 'collection_view_page', 'external_object_instance', 'bookmark', 'embed', 'file', 'pdf', 'code', 'callout']:
        lines.append(f'   PROPS: {json.dumps(props, ensure_ascii=False)}')
        if btype == 'page' and bid != page_id:
            subpages.append(bid)

with open('notion_parsed_all.md', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('\n'.join(lines))

print(f'Wrote {len(lines)} lines. Found subpages: {subpages}')

Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using hybrid search (semantic + keyword),
powered by the Entire search service.

Requires authentication via 'entire login' (GitHub device flow).

By default, results are scoped to the current repository. Use --all-repos to
search across all accessible repos.

Run without arguments to open an interactive search. Results are
displayed in an interactive table. Use --json for machine-readable output,
and add --compact for a trimmed per-result shape suited to agents (implies
--json): id, type, repo, branch, author, date, files touched, score, match
snippet, and a truncated title instead of the full prompt (repo hits add
description and checkpoint count). Fetch full detail
for a single result with 'entire checkpoint explain <id>', or add --full to
that command to pull the checkpoint's entire session transcript. For a
checkpoint hit from another GitHub repo, add --repo <owner/name> to
'entire checkpoint explain' (requires the full checkpoint ID; unrelated to
this command's --repo filter below).

CLI queries also support inline filters like author:<name>, date:<week|month>,
branch:<name>, repo:<owner/name>, and repo:* to search all accessible repos.

What is Entire?

104:

Entire is the git forge for AI-native teams. The Entire CLI captures every AI coding agent session, so the reasoning behind the code stays with the git repo, right next to your code. Then, Continuous Memory (Entire Graph + Entire Brain) turns those sessions into living knowledge for your agents. Your repo learns from every attempt, every fix, every decision, and your agents get smarter because of it.

Continuous Memory

Optional 318:
319:

Optional: only if you are building with Entire Graph/Brain.

320: 321:
322:

AInstall and activate entire-graph

323:

You or your agents can install the entire-graph plugin. Activate it once per repository:

324:
325:
Shell
326: 
entire plugin install graph
327: entire graph init-agents --repo .
328:
329: 330:

The second command creates .entire/graph-agent.md with the agent instructions, and adds a short block to your AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md telling your agents to use entire-graph.

331:

Commit those three files so it applies to your whole team, then start a fresh agent session. You'll know it worked when your agent's first move is entire-graph search instead of a grep.

332: 333:

Start using entire-graph

334:

Restart the agent so it picks up the new instructions, then ask in plain language: Where is request routing implemented? The agent runs graph queries, reads the code the graph points to, and answers with citations.

335:

To see what it saved you, run:

336:
337:
Shell
338: 
entire graph stats --repo .
339:
340: 341:

It reads your Claude Code session transcripts, counts how many times your agent used the graph instead of grepping and reading files, and estimates the tokens it saved. For how entire-graph works, installation, and troubleshooting, see the Graph docs .

342:
343: 344:
345:

BInstall entire-brain

346:

Make sure the Entire CLI and entire-graph are installed first (steps above).

347:
Without entire-graph, setup reports the semantic index as unavailable; sessions, docs and facts still work. Without the Entire CLI there are no sessions to read, and entire-brain falls back to code, docs and Git history.
348:
349:
Shell
350: 
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
351:
352: 353:

The script downloads a prebuilt binary, checks it against the release checksums, and registers it with the CLI as the entire-brain plugin.

354: 355:
356: Or build from source 357:

Needs Go 1.27+, Git 2.36+, the Entire CLI on your PATH, and a C compiler for Graph's tree-sitter bindings.

358:
359:
Shell
360: 
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain.git
361: cd entire-brain
362: ./scripts/install.sh
363:
364: 365:

This builds and registers entire-brain and entire-graph. It does not initialize a repository's memory or install the watcher. Then cd to the project repository where you want Brain and run:

366:
367:
Shell
368: 
entire brain setup

378:
379: 380:

This embeds your existing sessions (if any) and creates or updates the agent instructions at .entire/agent-guide.md. Rerunning the command replaces this file. It also updates AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md with references to the guide inside managed blocks; your text outside those blocks is preserved.

381:

Review the generated files and commit them together when the instructions should apply to your team. When entire-graph is installed, the guide tells agents to use entire-brain for prior decisions and entire-graph to locate and inspect code. Restart your agent or reload its repository instructions so it picks up the guide.

2: name: agy-customizations
3: description: >-
4:   Comprehensive guide and reference for the Antigravity Customization System.
5:   Use to explain how customizations work, their loading priority, discovery mechanisms,
6:   and to guide the creation of skills, rules, plugins, hooks, and MCP servers.
7: ---
8: 
9: # Antigravity Customization System Guide
10: 
11: The Antigravity Customization System allows you to tailor the agent's behavior,
12: teach it new workflows, enforce guidelines, and integrate it with external
13: tools. By customizing the agent, you can transition it from a general-purpose
14: assistant to an expert pair programmer specialized in your project's codebase
15: and processes.
16: 
17: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
18: 
19: ## Customization Types: Quick Reference
20: 
21: Choose the right customization type based on your goal:
22: 
23: Type            | Config File/Folder           | Scope                     | Best For                                                                                | Learn More
24: :-------------- | :--------------------------- | :------------------------ | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------
25: **Rules**       | `GEMINI.md`, `AGENTS.md`     | Contextual / Hierarchical | Enforcing coding styles, API restrictions, and local guidelines.                        | [Rules Guide](./docs/rules.md)
26: **Skills**      | `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`     | On-Demand (Progressive)   | Teaching the agent multi-step procedures, runbooks, and tool workflows.                 | [Skills Guide](./docs/skills.md)
27: **Plugins**     | `plugins/<name>/plugin.json` | Bundle                    | Packaging related skills, rules, and MCP configs into a single unit.                    | [Plugins Guide](./docs/plugins.md)
28: **Hooks**       | `hooks.json`                 | Lifecycle Event           | Running scripts/commands at specific agent lifecycle points (e.g., pre-tool execution). | [Hooks Guide](./docs/hooks.md)
29: **MCP Servers** | `mcp_config.json`            | Tool Integration          | Connecting the agent to external services and custom tool providers.                    | [MCP Guide](./docs/mcp_servers.md)
30: 
31: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
32: 
33: ## Customization Discovery and Locations
34: 
35: Antigravity automatically discovers your own customizations by traversing
36: specific directories. Built-in customizations are not found this way: the agent
37: config names the ones it mounts.
38: 
39: ### Discovery Locations
40: 
41: 1.  **Workspace Customizations** (Project-Specific):
42:     *   Path: `.agents/` (or `.agent/`, `_agents/`, `_agent/`) at the root of
43:         your project.
44:     *   Use this to share customizations with your team by checking them into
45:         version control (VCS).
46:     *   The agent walks from your current working directory up to the repository
47:         root (e.g., the folder containing `.git`) to find these directories.
48: 2.  **Directory & Project Rules** (Hierarchical):
49:     *   Paths: `GEMINI.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.agents/rules/*.md`
50:     *   As you open or edit files, the agent walks up from the file's directory
51:         to the repository root, loading all rules it finds.
52: 3.  **Global Configuration** (Machine-Local):
53:     *   Path: `~/.gemini/config/`
54:     *   Applies to all projects and workspaces run on your machine.
55: 
56: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
57: 
58: ## Loading Priority and Precedence
59: 
60: When multiple customizations are discovered, they are loaded and applied in a
61: specific order. If there are naming conflicts (e.g., two skills with the same
62: name), the higher-priority customization overrides the lower-priority one.
63: 
64: The priority order (from highest to lowest) is:
65: 
66: 1.  **Workspace Project**: Hierarchical discovery walking up from the CWD to the
67:     repository root.
68: 2.  **Declared Configurations**: Customizations explicitly listed in
69:     `skills.json` or `plugins.json` in your workspace.
70: 3.  **Global Discovery**: `~/.gemini/config/`
71: 4.  **Built-in Customizations**: Default skills bundled with the application,
72:     mounted by name rather than discovered.
73: 5.  **Global Declared Configurations**: Explicitly listed in global JSON
74:     configs.
75: 
76: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
77: 
78: ## How Customizations are Applied
79: 
80: ### Progressive Disclosure (Skills and Rules)
81: 
82: To prevent overwhelming the model's context window, Antigravity uses
83: **progressive disclosure**:
84: 
85: *   **Skills** are not loaded into the context window by default. Only their
86:     names and descriptions are injected. The full content of a skill is only
87:     loaded if the model (or the user) explicitly decides to activate it.
88: *   **Rules** with `trigger: model_decision` behave similarly. Only `always_on`
89:     rules are loaded unconditionally.
90: 
91: ### Deduplication
92: 
93: All customizations (especially rules) are deduplicated by their resolved file
94: paths. A rule file will never be injected more than once in a single
95: conversation turn, even if it matches multiple trigger conditions.
96: 
97: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
98: 
99: ## Advanced Management: JSON Configs
100: 
101: For customizations stored in non-standard locations, you can use `skills.json`
102: and `plugins.json` to explicitly register them and inherit from shared
103: configurations.
104: 
105: *   Learn how to configure these in the
106:     [JSON Configurations Guide](./docs/json_configs.md).

23: 
24: *   Rules are automatically deduplicated. Even if a rule is discovered via

# EHL Munich 2026 Grand Finale — Project & Agent Rules (Mandatory)

> **CRITICAL HACKATHON MANDATE (TUM.ai EHL Grand Finale, Oct 10–11, 2026):**
> Make effective use of **Entire** (`https://entire.io/`). Every AI coding agent (Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, OpenCode) working in this repository **MUST** capture its agent sessions, use Entire's Continuous Memory (Checkpoints, Search, Graph, Brain, and Trails), and ensure every Git commit is linked to session context. **Submissions without Entire checkpoints pushed to `origin` will NOT be accepted, and effective use of Entire is directly scored.**

- **Repository:** `https://github.com/vamshidharre/Tum.ai_GrandFinale.git` (`gh/vamshidharre/Tum.ai_GrandFinale`)
- **Event Guide:** `https://hack.entire.io/ehl-munich-2026/`
- **Entire Docs for LLMs:** `https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt` (MCP: `https://docs.entire.io/mcp`)

---

## 1. Golden Rules for All AI Agents (Claude, Codex, Antigravity, Cursor, Gemini)

1. **Never Bypass Entire Git Hooks:**
   - **NEVER** pass `--no-verify` to `git commit` or `git push`. Entire relies on Git hooks to attach agent session transcripts and push checkpoint refs (`[entire] Pushing checkpoint ref(s) to origin...`) on every commit and push.

9: # Atira Challenges
10: 
11: > Atira Challenges is a platform for agent hackathons in industrial sales. Teams build an agent system (one agent or several) that works through realistic business software, with any model through our proxy and their own tools. Each scored submission is reviewed automatically, run in an isolated sandbox on the public dataset, and ranked on a live leaderboard: eligible answers first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time. When the hackathon ends, every team's latest submission that passed review runs once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.
12: 
13: The public pages are also Markdown: the home page, Getting started, each challenge, its leaderboard and each team's profile. Add `.md` to the URL (`/index.md` for the home page) or send `Accept: text/markdown`. For runs, use the API or the CLI's MCP tools. Everything works with plain HTTP, so `curl` and the API guide are enough. Send your personal token (`atira token` prints it after `atira login`; plain curl can use the device flow in the API guide) or the run token in the `x-api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer`.
14: 
15: If you are a team's coding agent: install the CLI (`curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.sh | sh`, on Windows `irm https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.ps1 | iex`), have a team member run `atira login`, then add the CLI as your MCP server: `claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Claude Code) or `codex mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Codex). Its tools start test runs (`test_run`), wait for them (`wait_for_run`), show why one failed (`diagnose_run`, `run_logs`, `run_screenshot`, `run_inputs`) and submit (`submit`); [Debug runs from your coding agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md) lists them all. Run the agent locally against the public websites with `atira scout --env`, and start from the starter kit below. The agent you build must let a model choose where to go, what to search for and which documents matter, at run time: fixed scripts and crawlers that collect the websites for one model call are rejected in review, and so are values copied from the websites into the code.
16: 
17: Rules at a glance: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md
18: 
19: The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too. When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario.
20: 
21: The [leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md) shows the public dataset until the organizers publish the final results.
22: 
23: ## Start here
24: 
25: - [Getting started](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start.md): what you're building, your first run step by step with every command, the scouting logins for the websites, the rules of the game and how you're scored
26: - [The starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz): a minimal Python skeleton to start from (reading the run, the browsers over CDP, the hosted models; the agent is yours to build), as a gzipped tarball with `agent.json` at its root
27: 
28: ## Challenges
29: 
30: - [From RFQ to bid](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq.md): Your agent reads a public tender, finds the current specification, checks prices and stock in the ERP, looks up the approved discount in the sales inbox and submits one signed bid.
31: - [From RFQ to bid: leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md): the ranked results of scored submissions
32: - [From RFQ to bid: public dataset board](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md?dataset=public): every scored submission on the public dataset, also once the final results are live
33: 
34: ## Taking part
35: 
36: - [Participant guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/README.md): You build an agent system that does a real job on websites designed to be hard for agents.
37: - [Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md): Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and ranks everyone the same way.
38: - [How a run works](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md): A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge.
39: - [Building your agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/building-an-agent.md): Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes the decisions, at run time.
40: - [Fair play](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md): You submit an agentic system: one agent or several.
41: - [Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md): You submit your agent system as a gzipped tarball.
42: - [Demo day](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/demo-day.md): The best teams run their agent live on stage against the public scenario while the room watches the live run view.
43: - [FAQ and event details](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/faq.md)
44: 
45: ## API
46: 
47: - [OpenAPI 3.1 description](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/openapi.json): every participant endpoint, with credentials, request bodies (including the gzip upload), responses and errors
48: - [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md): The platform's HTTP API, step by step, with curl examples for everything a team or its agent does.

53: - [The CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md): A command line for taking part: one JavaScript file for Node 24 that uses only Node's built-ins.
54: - [Debug runs from your coding agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md): `atira mcp` makes the CLI an MCP server, so Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other coding agents can read your runs and debug them with you: find the failing step in the logs, see the browser's screen at that moment, check what the agent clicked and typed, then start the next test run.
55: - [Home](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/index.md): live totals, the top of the leaderboard and recent activity
56: - [Everything in one file](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/llms-full.txt): every public Markdown page and participant doc, concatenated

9: # Getting started: from sign-in to your first scored run
10: 
11: How to sign in, set up and test your agent, and get it on the leaderboard. Limits and scoring are at the bottom.
12: 
13: Fastest start: point Claude Code or Codex at this site. Paste this, and it installs the CLI, connects itself, and helps you build, test and submit:
14: 
15: ```text
16: Read https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/llms.txt, then set us up and help us build, test and submit an agent for this challenge.
17: ```
18: 
19: Web page: [https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start) · The challenge: [Markdown](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq.md) · For agents: [llms.txt](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/llms.txt) · [OpenAPI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/openapi.json) · [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md) · [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md)
20: 
21: ## What you're building
22: 
23: Your agent reads a public tender, finds the current specification, checks prices and stock in the ERP, looks up the approved discount in the sales inbox and submits one signed bid. Bring any frontier model, your own tools and prompts, up to four browsers in parallel; no human in the loop. Or use [ours](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start#models): unlimited Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare Clef inference. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair. Every scored submission runs once on the public dataset. Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time. When the hackathon ends, every team's latest submission that passed review runs once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order: performance on the private dataset, performance on the public dataset, and the elegance of the system.
24: 
25: ## Your first test run
26: 
27: Seven steps. The first five get your agent running against the websites. Step 6 tests it in the sandbox; step 7 puts it on the leaderboard.
28: 
29: ### 1. Sign in and form a team
30: 
31: [Sign in with GitHub](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/login?next=/team) and create a team of up to 5. Invite teammates by their GitHub username on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team); each invite works only for that account.
32: 
33: ### 2. Install the CLI and sign in
34: 
35: The [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md) is one file for Node 24; where Node 24 is missing, the installer offers a private copy for atira alone. `atira login` opens the browser, where you approve a token for this computer. On macOS and Linux, the second line puts `atira` on your PATH in this terminal; add it to your shell's startup file to keep it. Optional: connect your coding agent ([MCP](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md)), and it starts test runs, reads logs and sees each browser's screen itself. Or skip the install: point a coding agent at [https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/llms.txt](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/llms.txt).
36: 
37: macOS and Linux:
38: 
39: ```sh
40: curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.sh | sh
41: export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
42: atira login
43: ```
44: 
45: Windows, in PowerShell:
46: 
47: ```powershell
48: irm https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.ps1 | iex
49: atira login
50: ```
51: 
52: Optional: connect the coding agent you use (one line each):
53: 
54: ```sh
55: claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp   # Claude Code
56: codex mcp add atira -- atira mcp    # Codex
57: ```
58: 
59: ### 3. Scout the websites yourself
60: 
61: Logins for every website, with the public data. Click around as much as you like. None of it is scored. Rules at a glance: [Fair play](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md)
62: 
63: | Website | URL | Username | Password |
64: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
65: | Tender portal (Vergabeportal) | <https://atira-rfq-tender-portal.kyora.run> | `u_9c3cb06a5d21b197` | `uJC8-80QSb7rblI_k4tH` |
66: | Supplier portal (Lieferantenportal) | <https://atira-rfq-customer-portal.kyora.run> | `u_9c3cb06a5d21b197` | `k2sBynnldp0mqU4MviqI` |
67: | ERP | <https://atira-rfq-erp.kyora.run> | `u_9c3cb06a5d21b197` | `vuUcG2MsDEafLhoMjfS5` |
68: | Webmail (Werkpost) | <https://atira-rfq-mail.kyora.run> | `u_9c3cb06a5d21b197` | `ldPxYRdvI__aVKKqOWIy` |
69: 
70: ### 4. Choose your starting point
71: 
72: Fork the starter kit, or build your own from the [run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md) in any language, framework or architecture. The kit is a minimal Python skeleton, not an agent: it reads the run and submits an answer (`run.py`), attaches to the run's browsers (`browsers.py`), shows one call to each hosted model (`models.py`), and leaves your agent to `solve()` in `agent.py`.
73: 
74: macOS and Linux:
75: 
76: ```sh
77: mkdir my-agent
78: curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz | tar xz -C my-agent
79: ```
80: 
81: Windows, in PowerShell:
82: 
83: ```powershell
84: mkdir my-agent
85: curl.exe -fsSL -o starter-kit.tar.gz https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz
86: tar -xzf starter-kit.tar.gz -C my-agent
87: ```
88: 
89: ### 5. Develop locally
90: 
91: You need uv for the starter kit ([install uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/)); open a new terminal after installing it. Terminal 1: start the free models with `atira models proxy` and leave it open. Terminal 2: run the lines below. `atira scout --env` gives your agent the scouting logins, the way a run gets its own, and a browser opens on your machine. Nothing done here counts. With these logins, an answer entered on the tender portal is acknowledged but never counts. When it works, `atira test-run` runs it in the sandbox for up to 2 hours and opens the run live, with the score and full breakdown. Details: [how a run works](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md).
92: 
93: macOS and Linux:
94: 
95: ```sh
96: cd my-agent && uv sync && uv run playwright install chromium
97: eval "$(atira scout --env)"
98: uv run --no-sync python agent.py
99: ```
100: 
101: Windows, in PowerShell:
102: 
103: ```powershell
104: cd my-agent; uv sync; uv run playwright install chromium
105: atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression
106: uv run --no-sync python agent.py
107: ```
108: 
109: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare Clef work here too, with the same variables as in a run: [how to call them](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start#models).
110: 
111: ### 6. Test in the sandbox
112: 
113: The same sandbox as scored runs, on the public dataset: watch the browser and the live logs, and replay the recording afterwards. The hosted models need no key; a key of your own goes in a team secret on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team); only the timed run step gets it.
114: 
115: ```sh
116: atira test-run .
117: ```
118: 
119: ### 7. Submit
120: 
121: A coding agent reviews the package, it runs once on the public dataset, and the result lands on the [leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard). One submission in flight at a time; your best one holds your place, and your latest one that passed review goes into the final run. [Submitting in full](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md).
122: 
123: ```sh
124: atira submit .
125: ```
126: 
127: ## Unlimited Inference
128: 
129: We host Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare's Clef for this hackathon, free and with no usage cap. On your laptop, `atira models proxy` gives you a URL and key (setup on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team#team-models)). In test and scored runs it's set up for you. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair.
130: 
131: ### Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
132: 
133: #6 on the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/qwen3-8-flash-next) (open-weight, large models). Multimodal general-purpose LLM. Strong at reasoning, tool calls and reading pages and screenshots, with a 256k context, so it can plan, browse and write the answer.
134: 
135: - **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 32 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
136: - **Simulated pricing:**
137:   - Input: $0.15 / M tokens
138:   - Cached input: $0.016 / M tokens
139:   - Cache writes: Free
140:   - Output: $0.47 / M tokens
141: - **Precision:** [NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4) (NVIDIA's checkpoint)
142: 
143: Scales to zero when idle, but warm-up isn't counted toward a submission's time.
144: 
145: ```python
146: import os
147: from openai import OpenAI
148: 
149: qwen = OpenAI(
150:     base_url=os.environ["QWEN_BASE_URL"],
151:     api_key=os.environ["QWEN_API_KEY"],
152: )
153: reply = qwen.chat.completions.create(
154:     model="qwen",
155:     messages=[{
156:         "role": "user",
157:         "content": "Which button submits?",
158:     }],
159: )
160: ```
161: 
162: ### Cloudflare Clef
163: 
164: A multimodal decision model. Give it a state and up to 4 screenshots, then ask it questions: `choice` picks one of your options, `noul` gives the probability of yes, from 0 to 1, and `score` rates on a scale you set. See [Cloudflare's announcement](https://blog.cloudflare.com/clef-decision-models/) and [the benchmarks](https://clef-evals.workers-ai-mle.workers.dev). Worth a try for quick, low-stakes decisions, such as which link to open or whether a page is the right document, while the bigger model reads and reasons.
165: 
166: - **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 16 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
167: - **Simulated pricing:**
168:   - Input: $0.24 / M tokens
169:   - Output: Not priced
170: 
171: Scales to zero when idle, but warm-up isn't counted toward a submission's time.
172: 
173: ```sh
174: curl "$CLEF_BASE_URL/v1/decide" \
175:   -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLEF_API_KEY" \
176:   -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
177:   "state": {"page": "Checkout returns 502"},
178:   "questions": {"next": {
179:     "type": "choice",
180:     "instructions": "What next?",
181:     "criteria": {
182:       "retry": "Retry the request",
183:       "report": "Report the error"}}}}'
184: ```
185: 
186: In a run, `QWEN_BASE_URL` with `QWEN_API_KEY` and `CLEF_BASE_URL` with `CLEF_API_KEY` are set for you. On your machine, `atira models proxy` serves the same APIs on 127.0.0.1, so the same code works in both. Calls from your machine are free, recorded and never ranked. An idle model can take several minutes to wake on its first call, so use long timeouts.
187: 
188: ```sh
189: atira login   # once per computer
190: atira models proxy   # keep it running; it prints:
191: export QWEN_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8765/qwen/v1
192: export QWEN_API_KEY=local
193: export CLEF_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8765/clef
194: export CLEF_API_KEY=local
195: ```
196: 
197: Cost and time count toward your rank, and a call to these models costs a fraction of a frontier call. Use them for the easy steps.
198: 
199: If one fails mid-run, retry the call, as with any provider. If they were down for most of a run that then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count, and a scored run starts again once by itself.
200: 
201: ## Limits
202: 
203: What every scored run gets.
204: 
205: | Rule | What it means |
206: | --- | --- |
207: | Scored run | 20 minutes on the clock. Each submission runs once; one submission in flight per team. |
208: | Setup and network | Setup doesn't count toward your time: it has network access and up to 5 minutes to install what you need. The timed run reaches only the platform, the websites and the model proxy. |
209: | Models | Bring your own keys as team secrets, for Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI, Together, Fireworks. Every call goes through the run's proxy and is metered at the published prices. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare Clef are ours, unlimited. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair. |
210: | Browsers | At most 4 Chromium browsers at a time, provided by the sandbox; any number of tabs. |
211: | Sandbox | 4 vCPU, 8 GB memory and 30 GB disk on AMD Zen 5; 1280×800 screens. Node 24 with pnpm and bun, Python 3.12 with uv, Rust with cargo. |
212: | Package | Up to 20 MB compressed, with `agent.json` at the root. Its `"models"` lists the hosted models your agent calls (`["qwen", "clef"]` when absent); the run waits only for those to warm up, and `"models": []` starts it right after setup. |
213: | Fair play | The answer must come from the websites at run time, found by a model that does the navigating and deciding, not a fixed script or a crawler. A coding agent reviews every package. The final run uses a private dataset: the same jobs, bid rules and answer format, on different websites with other content and data. [Full rules](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md). |
214: | Team | Up to 5 people. |
215: 
216: ## How you're scored
217: 
218: Every scored run gets a quality and an eligibility verdict; the platform measures its cost and time.
219: 
220: - **Quality:** 0 to 100. Every field of the bid is compared with the one correct answer: tender reference, positions, materials, quantities, unit prices, lead times, discount and total, each position's base price and surcharge per piece, packaging, allocated project bonus, and whether the total adds up.
221: - **Eligibility:** The right tender reference; a wrong decision loses quality points but other correct fields keep their credit. A bid that is not eligible ranks after every eligible one.
222: 
223: Order: Eligible first → Quality ↓ → Cost × time ↑.
224: 
225: Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality. At equal quality, the lower product of cost and time wins, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time as at least 1 s, so among free runs the faster one wins.
226: 
227: On the leaderboard's plot, each dot is a team, quality against cost or time. The dotted line is the Pareto front. The quickest and cheapest passing solution might also get a small prize ;) [Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md) has every point.
228: 
229: ## Public and private data
230:

106: ## Bid rules
107: 
108: The brief states these rules in full. Together they define exactly one correct answer.
109: 
110: 1. **Quantity:** The tender quantity, overridden by the latest clarification that changes that position.
111: 2. **Requirement:** The position's requirement in the specification revision marked current.
112: 3. **Material:** The active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification match exactly. If a position has none, the answer is no bid.
113: 4. **Unit price:** The price condition valid on the scenario date, at the highest quantity scale reached, minus the approved discount, rounded half-up to the cent.
114: 5. **Discount:** The most recent approval from the sales director for this exact tender; otherwise 0 %.
115: 6. **Lead time:** The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
116: 7. **Total:** The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
117: 8. **Decision:** Bid, with one entry per tender position; no bid with no positions and a total of 0 when a material is missing.
118: 9. **Partial submission:** Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
119: 10. **Finding records:** The specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
120: 11. **Agent requirement:** A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
121: 12. **Commercial clauses:** A tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
122: 13. **Withdrawn answers:** A tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer's quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
123: 14. **Scoped amendments:** After selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
124: 15. **Shared stock:** Sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
125: 16. **Conditional discount:** The latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
126: 17. **Units:** Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
127: 18. **Pricing breakdown:** Base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
128: 19. These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
129: 20. **Technical derivation:** For a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
130: 21. **Authority and time:** Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
131: 22. **Currency:** The valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
132: 23. **Packaging:** Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
133: 24. **Delivery:** Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.
134: 25. **Shared setup:** Q&A identifies pool members; ERP gives allocation mass (distinct from surcharge mass); the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee. Allocate by quantity × allocation mass using the cent-allocation rule in that mail. Add each allocation to that position's ordinary setup fee. Report surcharge_per_unit BEFORE discount, excluding packaging and bonus.
135: 26. **Project bonus:** The finance mail gives marginal percentage bands. Compute the eligible undiscounted EUR goods total, apply each band only to its portion, round the aggregate credit HALF_UP to cents, then allocate proportionally to eligible line goods values using largest remainders in cents (ties: ascending position identifier). Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.
136: 27. **Final price:** Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
137: 28. **Metal indices:** Select the latest exact-reference Preisindizes message from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. If the code lists validity windows, use the rate whose inclusive window contains the scenario date, not the last rate listed.
138: 29. **Scoring in bid cases:** Decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, positions 75 minus any additional checks, correct total 5, arithmetic consistency 5. When present, the withdrawn Q&A quantity and date-selected metal-index checks earn 5 points each. Within each equally weighted position: material 20%, quantity 15%, base price 15%, surcharge 10%, packaging 10%, project bonus 10%, final unit price 10%, delivery 10%. Each field is independent; optional breakdown fields can be blank. No-bid scoring is unchanged.

140: ## How a run works
141: 
142: Develop on your machine against the public websites with the scouting logins (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox: `atira test-run` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live, or drop the package on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). A test run lasts up to 2 hours on the public data and returns its score with the full breakdown. In the commands, `$ATIRA_TOKEN` holds your personal token (sign in with `atira login`, then `atira token`).
143: 
144: 1. **Start.** The run issues a token, the task brief and fresh logins for every website.
145: 2. **Read.** Your agent reads the brief, the rules and the answer format from the API.
146: 3. **Work the websites.** It works through the 4 websites in a real browser and gathers the facts.
147: 4. **Submit.** It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.
148: 5. **Scored.** The answer is checked against the one correct answer; quality, cost and time are recorded.

259: ```sh
260: atira login   # once per computer
261: atira models proxy   # keep it running; it prints:
262: export QWEN_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8765/qwen/v1
263: export QWEN_API_KEY=local
264: export CLEF_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8765/clef
265: export CLEF_API_KEY=local
266: ```
267: 
268: Cost and time count toward your rank, and a call to these models costs a fraction of a frontier call. Use them for the easy steps.
269: 
270: If one fails mid-run, retry the call, as with any provider. If they were down for most of a run that then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count, and a scored run starts again once by itself.
271: 
272: ## Submitting
273: 
274: A submission is your agent as a gzipped tarball. It is reviewed automatically, then run once in the sandbox on the public dataset, and that score ranks your team. Submit as often as you like, one at a time; your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard, and your latest one that passed review goes into the final run.
275: 
276: ### agent.json
277: 
278: ```json
279: {
280:   "setup": ["uv", "sync"],
281:   "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"],
282:   "models": ["qwen"]
283: }
284: ```
285: 
286: Put `agent.json` at the root of the tarball, next to your code and its dependency file. Up to 20 MB compressed. `setup` installs dependencies with network access, within 5 minutes that don't count toward your time; `run` is timed and reaches only the platform and the websites. `"browsers": 1–4` (default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts, each on its own screen. `"models"` lists the hosted models your agent calls; the run waits only for those to warm up (for all of them when it's absent). Node 24 with pnpm and bun, Python 3.12 with uv, and Rust with cargo are installed. The [starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal skeleton to start from.
287: 
288: ### Upload
289: 
290: ```sh
291: tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
292: curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
293:   -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" \
294:   -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
295:   "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions"
296: ```
297: 
298: Or drop the tarball on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). Upload it as a test run first to watch it work in the sandbox: its browser live, its logs, and a recording afterwards.
299: 
300: ### Test run first
301: 
302: The same tarball as a test run: one run in the scored-run sandbox on the public data, with live browser frames, logs and a recording.
303: 
304: ```sh

316: ```

322: ```
323: 
324: ## Scoring and ranking
325: 
326: Every submission is measured on its run in the sandbox.
327: 
328: - **Quality:** 0 to 100. Every field of the bid is compared with the one correct answer: tender reference, positions, materials, quantities, unit prices, lead times, discount and total, each position's base price and surcharge per piece, packaging, allocated project bonus, and whether the total adds up.
329: - **Eligibility:** The right tender reference; a wrong decision loses quality points but other correct fields keep their credit. A bid that is not eligible ranks after every eligible one.
330: - **Cost:** Every model call goes through the proxy and is priced per model. There is no budget: at equal quality, cost × time decides.
331: - **Time:** Wall-clock time from the start of the run until the answer is accepted. It weighs as much as cost: halving either halves cost × time.
332: 
333: Order: Eligible first → Quality ↓ → Cost × time ↑.
334: 
335: Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality. At equal quality, the lower product of cost and time wins, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time as at least 1 s, so among free runs the faster one wins.
336: 
337: ## Leaderboard
338: 
339: **Public dataset.** Eligible first, then quality, then cost × time. The top ten; the [full leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md) has every team.
340: 
341: No team has a scored submission yet. Test runs don't appear here.
342: 
343: ## Fair play
344: 
345: Your agent has to find the answer itself.
346: 
347: - Your system must work the answer out from the websites at run time, with a model doing the navigating and deciding. A coding agent reviews every package; hardcoded answers, fixed scripts and crawlers are rejected.
348: - Bring your own model key for Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI, Together, Fireworks, kept as a team secret. Every call goes through the run's proxy and is metered at the published prices. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare Clef are ours, unlimited. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair. The sandbox reaches the platform and the websites, nothing else.
349: - At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up to 4 in agent.json ("browsers"), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The sandbox stops any other browser your agent starts.
350: - One submission in flight per team. Submit again once it has finished.
351: 
352: Rules at a glance: [Fair play](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md)

9: # Answers and scoring
10: 
11: > In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
12: 
13: Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
14: ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
15: websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
16: isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
17: on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).
18: 
19: ## Per run
20: 
21: - **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
22: - **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
23:   a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
24: - **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
25: - **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.
26: 
27: A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
28: is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.
29: 
30: ## Leaderboard
31: 
32: Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
33: keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
34: complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
35: the run's own value.
36: 
37: 1. Eligible before ineligible.
38: 2. Higher quality.
39: 3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
40:    as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
41:    time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
42: 4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.
43: 
44: On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
45: the teams no other eligible team beats on both.
46: 
47: Test runs on the public scenario `public-1` show the points for each part of the answer, never the expected
48: values. Scored runs show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.
49: 
50: ## Final run
51: 
52: When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
53: answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
54: 
55: ## Winners
56: 
57: We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:
58: 
59: 1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
60: 2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
61: 3. The elegance of the system.
62: 
63: It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
64: latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
65: publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
66: public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
67: `leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).
68: 
69: ## RFQ scoring
70: 
71: The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
72: `base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
73: ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
74: project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
75: The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
76: omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.
77: 
78: | Part (a bid) | Points |
79: | --- | --- |
80: | Decision | 5 |
81: | Tender reference | 5 |
82: | Discount percent | 5 |
83: | Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
84: | Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
85: | Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
86: | Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
87: | Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |
88: 
89: 
90: For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
91: points but leaves the other fields their credit.
92: 
93: Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
94: one position's share each.
95: 
96: ## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
97: 
98: The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
99: Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
100: `atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
101: When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
102: Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
103: counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
104: It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
105: Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
106: Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
107: on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.
108: 
109: Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
110: the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
111: rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.

9: # Fair play
10: 
11: **Rules at a glance**
12: 
13: You submit an agentic system: one agent or several. In the sandbox it does the whole job on its own: finds what it needs on the four websites, works out the bid and submits it. Nobody helps it during a run.
14: 
15: **Not allowed**
16: 
17: - **Hardcoding:** copying values from the websites into your package (prices, material numbers, totals, discounts, logins, TANs), including in prompts and notes, also as defaults or fallbacks. Using what the task brief tells every team, like the sales director's mailbox, is fine.
18: - **Pre-solving:** working out the answer yourself, or having an AI assistant do it, and putting the result in your package. Exploring the sites with an assistant is fine.
19: - **Scripts instead of agents:** a fixed click path, or a crawler that grabs everything for one model call. A model has to choose where to go, what to search for and what matters.
20: - **Outside help during a run:** contacting anything besides our platform and the four websites, calling a model other than through our proxy (your own API keys work through it), running a model inside the sandbox, or starting your own browsers (use the up to 4 provided). Setup may install dependencies.
21: 
22: **How it's checked:** an AI reviewer reads every submitted package before its scored run. Unclear cases are flagged and stay off the leaderboard until an organizer has looked. The final runs on websites and data your system hasn't seen.
23: 
24: The details follow.
25: 
26: ## Allowed
27: 
28: - Any agent design; the free hosted models, or any provider and model with your own key, through the proxy; any
29:   amount of tokens.
30:   The proxy forwards your calls unchanged and measures them: reported usage is metered at the published model
31:   prices, and an upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. See [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)
32:   for SDK configuration.
33: - Keeping your model key as a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets) rather than in your package.
34: - Your own code, prompts and tools; open-source libraries installed during setup.
35: - Using what you learned with the scouting logins and in test runs about how the websites work.
36: - Up to 4 browsers at a time: ask for them with `"browsers"` in `agent.json` and use as many tabs and browser
37:   contexts inside them as you like.
38: 
39: ## Not allowed
40: 
41: - Hardcoding values copied from the public scenario or its websites into code, config, prompts or notes, including defaults and fallbacks: tender references, material numbers, prices, totals, discounts, logins and TANs. Facts the task brief states for every scenario, such as the sales director's mailbox, are
42:   rules you may use.
43: - A scripted solution. Your agent system must be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the
44:   information and makes the decisions. Code can help it (browser control, parsing, arithmetic, checks, reading a
45:   page or document the model chose, paging through results it asked for), and several agents and browsers may work
46:   in parallel. Rejected: a fixed script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback,
47:   and a crawler that collects the websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
48: - Bundling or running a local model, or reaching any model other than through the proxy.
49: - Contacting hosts other than the API and the challenge's websites, or trying to get data out of the sandbox.
50: - Starting browsers of your own in the sandbox, headless ones included. At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up
51:   to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start others.
52:   On your own machine (developing with the scouting logins) your agent starts its own browsers; that is up to you.
53: - Attacking the platform, the websites, the sandbox or other teams; sharing scored-run data.
54: 
55: ## How it is checked
56: 
57: - **Package review before any scored run:** an AI code reviewer, a coding agent that reads your whole package in an
58:   isolated VM. Outcomes: passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged package still runs and scores, but its
59:   result stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it
60:   marked "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Notes and docs addressed to the reviewer are not evidence of compliance
61:   and do not count against you on their own. Instructions trying to steer the reviewer's verdict do.
62:   The reviewer's reasons stay with the organizers: your team reads "Flagged by the reviewing agent" or "Rejected by
63:   the reviewing agent". Someone from Atira looks at flagged packages shortly and unflags a misdetection; if you think
64:   a reject is one, contact the Atira team.
65: - **The organizers decide flagged packages, and can look at any submission:** they pass it, add an internal note
66:   (this changes nothing you or the leaderboard see) or disqualify it. A disqualified submission and its runs read
67:   "disqualified": it leaves the leaderboard and the final run, its runs still going stop, and your team page shows the
68:   organizers' reason.
69: - **Hardcoded values:** the reviewer rejects copied scenario values in code or config, even in defaults or fallbacks.
70: - **The final run** uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a
71:   supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software,
72:   with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently
73:   across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. That run weighs most when we pick the
74:   winners, so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
75: - **The sandbox** reaches only our API and the websites, so every model call passes the proxy and is measured.
76:   Your team secrets reach only the timed run step and are redacted from its logs.
77: - **Website logins** exist only for a live run and stop working when it ends.
78: - **Browsers:** the sandbox stops any browser your agent starts beyond the ones it asked for and notes it in the
79:   run's logs: `[platform] stopped a browser the agent started`.
80: - **Everything measured** (tokens, cost, time, the answer) is recorded by the platform, never reported by you.
81: 
82: Breaking these rules gets the submission rejected before it runs, or removed later; repeated or deliberate attempts
83: get the team disqualified.
84: 
85: ## Flagged results
86: 
87: A flagged result stays off the public leaderboard until an organizer passes it. **Show flagged** on the leaderboard
88: lists flagged results, without a rank.

### 1. Best Team Name Ideas (Industrial AI + Hydraulics + Multi-Agent Theme)

Since the challenge is **Atira: From RFQ to Bid** (building an autonomous multi-browser AI sales engineer for a **German hydraulics cylinder manufacturer** that navigates a Vergabeportal, Lieferantenportal, SAP-style ERP, and Werkpost Webmail), here are the best team names:

2. **`Stroke of Genius`** *(Double meaning: hydraulic cylinder **stroke** / *nutzbarer Weg* + AI brilliance)*

### 2. Understanding the Game & Scoring Mechanics (How We Win)

#### What the Agent Must Do at Runtime
Given one public tender for hydraulic cylinders across **4 live websites** (each with its own login in `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS`):
1. **Tender Portal (`tender-portal` / Vergabeportal):** Pass cookie walls/flaky pages, express interest, download/read tender documents (iframes/ZIPs), extract the Bill of Quantities (positions, units like `Satz` vs pieces), parse **Bidder Q&A** (withdrawn answers `zurückziehen`, quantity overrides, scoped technical amendments, commercial `Konditionsgruppe`, packaging tariff keys, delivery commitment keys, shared setup `Rüstpools`), and finally **fill the Bid Configurator & sign with a TAN**.
2. **Supplier Portal (`customer-portal` / Lieferantenportal):** Navigate document revisions to find the **current** specification revision (watch out: opens oldest revision first!), paginate requirement tables, and extract technical specs (`bore`, `stroke` / `nutzbarer Weg`, `pressure`, `mounting`, `certification`, `Kataloggruppe`, pieces per `Satz`).
3. **ERP (`erp`):** Navigate SAP-style transaction codes, F4 search popups, and short session timeouts to look up `Kataloggruppe` (narrowing to $\le 20$ results), find the **active** matching material (`bore`, `stroke`, `pressure`, `mounting`, `certification`), stock levels, lead times (stock vs production), carton sizes, allocation mass, surcharge mass, and price conditions (currency, FX key, validity window on the scenario date, quantity scales).
4. **Webmail (`mail` / Werkpost):** Search inbox + archive (AND search) for the **exact tender reference** and latest records $\le$ scenario date from authorized senders:
   - Sales director discount approval (and conditional minimum undiscounted net order value threshold)
   - `Technikfreigabe` (`technik@...` — per-end stroke reserve for `nutzbarer Weg`)
   - `Konditionsregeln` (`kalkulation@...` — whether discount applies to base only, base + mass surcharge, or neither)
   - `Preisindizes` (`kalkulation@...` — metal index rates valid on scenario date)
   - `Rüstpools` (`kalkulation@...` — shared setup pool fee & cent-allocation rule)
   - `Verpackungstarife` (`logistik@...` — packaging tariffs)
   - `Terminfreigabe` (`logistik@...` — delivery commitment ceilings)
   - `Devisenfixing` (`finanzen@...` — FX conversion rates to EUR)
   - `Projektbonus` (`finanzen@...` — marginal percentage bands & largest-remainder cent allocation)
   - **Signing TAN** (sent after entering the bid in the tender portal configurator).

#### How Winners Are Ranked
$$\text{Rank Order: } \mathbf{Eligible\ First} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Quality\ (0\text{--}100)\ \downarrow} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Cost \times Time\ \uparrow}$$

  2. **Performance on the Public Dataset (`public-1` Leaderboard)**
  3. **Elegance of the System**
- **Fair Play / AI Package Reviewer:** Every submission tarball is inspected by an AI reviewer before running. **Zero hardcoded scenario values**, **no fixed click paths**, and **no blind crawlers** that dump whole sites into one prompt. The LLM must genuinely decide navigation targets, searches, and document selection at runtime, while deterministic Python tools/helpers assist with extraction, pagination, and exact `Decimal` math.

### 3. Our Winning Architecture & Hillclimbing Strategy

To dominate **both** the Public Leaderboard (`Quality = 100`, minimal `Cost × Time`) and the **Private Dataset Final Run** (generalization to unseen UI layouts), here is our 4-pillar architecture:

#### Why This Wins on Quality, Speed, Cost, and Private Dataset:
1. **4 Parallel Browsers (`"browsers": 4` in `agent.json`):**
   - The sandbox gives us up to **4 Chromium instances** on `:1`–`:4` via `CDP_URLS`.
   - Instead of visiting 4 websites sequentially (which takes $4\times$ longer), we spawn **4 parallel async Playwright worker agents** at $t = 0$ to log in and explore the Tender Portal, Supplier Portal, ERP, and Webmail simultaneously, cutting wall-clock time `T` by 60–70%!
2. **Free Hosted `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` + `Cloudflare Clef` Hybrid Routing:**
   - Atira hosts **Qwen3.8-Flash-Next** (\$0.15/M input, \$0.016/M cached input, \$0.47/M output, 32 concurrent calls) and **Cloudflare Clef** (\$0.24/M input, $0 output).

3. **DOM-Snapshot + Semantic Action Loop (Zero Hardcoded Selectors):**
   - Because the **Private Dataset** changes the website software, layout, navigation, and site names, our browser tool gives the LLM a compact interactive DOM accessibility tree (numbered interactive elements `[1] <button> ...`, `[2] <input> ...`, tables, iframes, download hooks) + automatic popup/cookie/session-timeout recovery.
   - The model decides what to click/search/open based on semantics, not hardcoded CSS selectors, guaranteeing **Private Dataset survival**.
4. **100% Exact `Decimal` Calculation Engine (Zero LLM Math Errors):**
   - LLMs are great at extracting structured facts from messy German tables/emails, but terrible at multi-step cent allocation (`ROUND_HALF_UP`, largest-remainder cent distribution for `Projektbonus` and `Rüstpools`).
   - Per Rule 11 (*"Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms"*), our agent extracts structured facts into a validated Pydantic ledger and runs a heavily unit-tested Python `decimal.Decimal` pricing engine that implements all **29 Bid Rules** to the exact cent.
5. **Partial-Submission Fail-Safe:**
   - If any edge case occurs or the 20-minute clock gets close, our agent never dies with 0 points — it uses the partial submission / omission mechanism if needed and always completes the **TAN signature** so every earned point counts.

9: # Building your agent
10: 
11: Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes
12: the decisions, at run time. How is up to you: drive the browser through the DOM, through pixels, or both; use one
13: model or several, in parallel if you like; give the model tools and helpers for the browser, parsing, arithmetic and
14: checks. The model chooses where to go, what to search for and which documents matter. Rejected in review: a fixed
15: script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback, and a crawler that collects the
16: websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
17: 
18: ## The browser
19: 
20: In the sandbox a headful Chromium runs on the desktop (`DISPLAY=:1`, 1280×800) with CDP on
21: `127.0.0.1:9222`.
22: 
23: - **DOM agents:** attach with Playwright (`chromium.connect_over_cdp(CDP_URL)`) or any CDP client.
24: - **Pixel agents:** take screenshots and send mouse and keyboard input to the desktop (`xdotool` and
25:   ImageMagick's `import` are installed), for example to drive Claude's computer-use tool.
26: - **Locally:** without `CDP_URL`, launch your own Chromium. The websites are the same: `eval "$(atira scout --env)"`
27:   gives your agent the scouting logins in `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS`, the way a run gets its logins.
28: 
29: ### Several browsers
30: 
31: To work on several websites at once, ask for up to four browsers in `agent.json`:
32: 
33: ```json
34: {"setup": ["npm", "ci"], "run": ["node", "agent.js"], "browsers": 2}
35: ```
36: 
37: Each is its own Chromium on its own screen (browser n on `DISPLAY=:n`), and `CDP_URLS` lists their CDP URLs in
38: order (`CDP_URL` stays the first). With Playwright:
39: 
40: ```javascript
41: import { chromium } from "playwright"
42: 
43: const sites = JSON.parse(process.env.CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS)
44: const browsers = await Promise.all(JSON.parse(process.env.CDP_URLS).map((url) => chromium.connectOverCDP(url)))
45: const pages = browsers.map((browser) => browser.contexts()[0].pages()[0])
46: await Promise.all([pages[0].goto(sites[0].url), pages[1].goto(sites[1].url)])
47: ```
48: 
49: At most 4 browsers run at a time. Use tabs (`context.newPage()`) and browser contexts (`browser.newContext()`)
50: inside them as freely as you like, but don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included: the sandbox stops
51: them and says so in the run's logs. A test run shows its browsers side by side while it runs and keeps a recording
52: of each. Locally there is no `CDP_URLS`: on your machine your agent starts its own browsers.
53: 
54: ## Models
55: 
56: The hosted models are free to use. Every run gets `QWEN_BASE_URL` and `QWEN_API_KEY` for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an
57: OpenAI-compatible chat model with tool calls and images; on your machine `atira scout --env` sets the same variables,
58: pointed at `atira models proxy`. You can also bring your own key for any provider through the metering proxy;
59: [how cost is measured](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#how-cost-is-measured) has the details. After quality you are ranked on cost × time, so a cheaper model or a faster run that gets the answer right moves you
60: up.
61: 
62: ## What makes it hard, on purpose
63: 
64: The websites are designed to trip agents up: cookie walls, flaky error pages that need a retry, expiring sessions
65: that send you back to the login, documents inside iframes and ZIP files, popups that close themselves, paging and
66: "load more" buttons, look-alike records, superseded versions shown first, a timezone that is not yours. Treat
67: every page as adversarial and verify what you read.
68: 
69: ## Tips
70: 
71: - Read the brief's rules carefully: they define the one correct answer.
72: - Keep what the model reads small: page text without duplicated labels, only the parts you need.
73: - Use prompt caching for your system prompt and tool definitions.
74: - Re-read a page after every action that changes it; pages update asynchronously.
75: - Drive four browsers in parallel, one per website (`"browsers": 4`, see [Several browsers](#several-browsers)):
76:   reading the four sites at once speeds up each run and your iteration, at the cost of more complex code.
77: - Validate your answer against `answer_schema` before sending it; a `400` costs only time.
78: - Submit before the clock runs out: a scored run has 20 minutes (`expires_at` in the run). Every part of the answer
79:   scores on its own, so have your agent submit its best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
80:   searching; a run that ends without an answer scores 0.
81: - Develop against the public websites locally (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox (`atira test-run`):
82:   a test run shows the full score breakdown, so use it to find what your agent gets wrong.
83: - Work the answer out from the websites: the final run, which weighs most for the winners, uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it.
84:

87: [`starter-kit/`](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal Python skeleton, not an agent: it reads the run and
88: submits an answer, attaches to the run's browsers over CDP with Playwright, and shows one call to each hosted model.
89: Your agent goes in `solve()` in `agent.py`; out of the box it exits without an answer. Start from it or from scratch.
