9: # How a run works
10: 
11: > In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
12: 
13: A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
14: logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
15: scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
16: logins.
17: 
18: ## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox
19: 
20: RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.
21: 
22: 1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
23:    `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
24:    `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
25:    `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
26:    `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
27:    Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
28:    `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
29:    `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
30:    provider takes your own key.
31:    Nothing done with these logins counts.
32:    A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
33: 2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
34:    opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
35:    20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
36:    score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.
37: 
38: ## Inside a run
39: 
40: 1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
41:    returns:
42:    - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
43:    - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
44:    - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
45:      `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
46:    - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
47:    - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
48:    - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
49:      provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
50:    Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
51: 2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
52:    go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
53:    provider's with your own key (below).
54: 3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
55:    `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
56:    forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
57:    - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
58:      it again.
59:    - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
60:      returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.
61: 
62: Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
63: (`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
64: front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.
65: 
66: ## LLM calls
67: 
68: Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
69: Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
70: own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
71: API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.
72: 
73: The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:
74: 
75: ```
76: $API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
77: ```
78: 
79: `llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:
80: 
81: | Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
82: | --- | --- | --- |
83: | `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
84: | `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
85: | `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
86: | `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
87: | `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
88: | `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
89: | `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
90: | `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
91: | `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
92: | `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |
93: 
94: The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
95: each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
96: (messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.
97: 
98: ### Your key
99: 
100: Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
101: (OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
102: unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
103: not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.
104: 
105: With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
106: `OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
107: as `x-api-key`:
108: 
109: ```python
110: from openai import OpenAI
111: 
112: client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
113: ```
114: 
115: A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
116: the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:
117: 
118: ```python
119: import os
120: from google import genai
121: 
122: client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
123:     http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
124: ```
125: 
126: ```javascript
127: import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"
128: 
129: const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
130:   httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
131: ```
132: 
133: A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
134: organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
135: key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
136: start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.
137: 
138: **Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
139: `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
140: (prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
141: for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
142: `x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
143: `401`.
144: 
145: A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
146: context.
147: 
148: ### How cost is measured
149: 
150: Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
151: provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
152: An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
153: `"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
154: that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
155: a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
156: providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
157: chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
158: an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
159: early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
160: endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
161: fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.
162: 
163: The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
164: charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.
165: 
166: ### Team secrets
167: 
168: Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
169: `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:
170: 
171: ```sh
172: curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
173:   --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
174: curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
175: curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
176: ```
177: 
178: Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
179: Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
180: cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
181: `CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.
182: 
183: ## Scored run
184: 
185: Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
186: ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
187: [Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
188: a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
189: `127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:
190: 
191: - **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
192: - **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
193: - **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
194:   and the websites.
195: - gcc, make, git, curl and jq.
196: 
197: 1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
198: 2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
199:    to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
200:    run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
201:    never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
202:    them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
203:    `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
204:    right after setup:
205: 
206:    ```json
207:    {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": []}
208:    ```
209: 
210:    Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
211:    `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
212:    whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.
213: 
214:    **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.
215:    If our models were down for most of the run (from the first failed call on, a 5xx from our model or a lost
216:    connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run
217:    then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count toward ranking or
218:    any limit, and a scored run starts again once by itself. A
219:    run that answered keeps its result.
220: 3. **Run (timed):** your `run` command starts with this environment. The clock starts here.
221: 
222: | Variable | Value |
223: | --- | --- |
224: | `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the API; read your task at `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` |
225: | `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | the run token |
226: | `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with this run's logins, as JSON: the same as `access` |
227: | `LLM_PROXY_URL` | `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` |
228: | `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | for each model the platform hosts (`GET /v1/models/status`; the start page names them): its base URL through the proxy, under `$LLM_PROXY_URL/<provider>`, and the run token as its key |
229: | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
230: | `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
231: | `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google`; set the Gemini SDK's HTTP base URL explicitly as above |
232: | `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL`, `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral`, `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
233: | your [team secrets](#team-secrets) | for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` with your own key |
234: | `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222`, browser 1 |
235: | `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: `["http://127.0.0.1:9222"]` for one browser |
236: | `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started: `1` unless `agent.json` asks for more |
237: | `DISPLAY` | `:1`, browser 1's screen; browser n is on `:n` |
238: | `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` (and lowercase) | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`, the only way out of the sandbox |
239: | `NO_PROXY` | `localhost,127.0.0.1` (CDP stays local) |
240: 
241: The platform sets no API key variables of its own, except the run-token placeholder for a provider the
242: organizers pay for (above). `setup` runs first, with network (install your dependencies there) but without the
243: run's variables or your team secrets, and nothing it starts survives into the run. The run itself reaches only our API and the challenge's websites,
244: through that proxy; Chromium is already configured to use it. A scored run of RFQ has 20 minutes; a run that
245: ends without an answer scores 0.
246: 
247: ## Browsers
248: 
249: The sandbox starts one browser unless `agent.json` asks for more, up to four:
250: 
251: ```json
252: {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "browsers": 3}
253: ```
254: 
255: `browsers` is a whole number from 1 to 4; anything else rejects the package with
256: `Invalid agent.json: browsers: must be a whole number from 1 to 4`. Browser n is its own headful Chromium with its
257: own profile, on display `:n` (1280×800) with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on port 9221 + n (9222 to 9225), behind
258: the same proxy as browser 1. All of them are ready before the clock starts. `CDP_URL` stays browser 1, `CDP_URLS` lists all of
259: them in order, and `BROWSER_COUNT` says how many there are. With three:
260: 
261: | Variable | Value |
262: | --- | --- |
263: | `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222` |
264: | `CDP_URLS` | `["http://127.0.0.1:9222","http://127.0.0.1:9223","http://127.0.0.1:9224"]` |
265: | `BROWSER_COUNT` | `3` |
266: 
267: **At most 4 browsers run at a time:** ask for up to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts
268: inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The scored sandbox enforces it:
269: any other browser the agent starts is stopped within seconds, and the run's logs say so with
270: `[platform] stopped a browser the agent started: at most 4 run at a time; use the browsers from CDP_URLS`. Every
271: browser then is one the platform can show and record: test runs show them side by side while they run, with a
272: recording of each afterwards.
273: 
274: On your own machine, developing with the scouting logins, `CDP_URLS` is not set and your agent starts its own
275: browsers.

9: # Debug runs from your coding agent
10: 
11: > In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
12: 
13: `atira mcp` makes the CLI an MCP server, so Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other coding agents can read your runs
14: and debug them with you: find the failing step in the logs, see the browser's screen at that moment, check what the
15: agent clicked and typed, then start the next test run. It uses the CLI's sign-in, so there is nothing new to set up.
16: 
17: ## Set it up
18: 
19: Install the CLI and sign in once ([CLI guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md)):
20: 
21: ```sh
22: curl -fsSL $API/install.sh | sh
23: atira login
24: ```
25: 
26: Then add the server to your coding agent:
27: 
28: ```sh
29: claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp     # Claude Code
30: codex mcp add atira -- atira mcp      # Codex
31: ```
32: 
33: Other clients (Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Desktop, ...) take the usual `mcpServers` entry:
34: 
35: ```json
36: { "mcpServers": { "atira": { "command": "atira", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
37: ```
38: 
39: For Codex you can also write it in `~/.codex/config.toml`:
40: 
41: ```toml
42: [mcp_servers.atira]
43: command = "atira"
44: args = ["mcp"]
45: ```
46: 
47: If your editor can't find `atira`, give its full path: `command -v atira` prints it. `ATIRA_TOKEN` works instead of
48: the stored sign-in, and `atira mcp --help` prints these lines.
49: 
50: ## Tools
51: 
52: | Tool | What it does | About |
53: | --- | --- | --- |
54: | `challenge_brief` | The challenge: task, websites, rules and limits, run contract, scoring and answer schema | 6k tokens |
55: | `list_runs` | Your team's recent test and scored runs: status, quality, cost, time and package | 50 tokens a run |
56: | `get_run` | One run: status and failure, queue place or warm-up while it waits, phases, package, model calls by model with failures and queue waits, points per field, recordings, answer, run page | 1–2k |
57: | `diagnose_run` | Why a run failed and whether to rerun it as it is: the failure class, the last 20 stdout and stderr lines, model errors, idle stretches over 60 s, browsers whose screen froze | 2–3k |
58: | `run_logs` | Log lines in time order, by time (`from`, `to`), stream, text (`grep`) and `browser`; `tail` for the last lines; page by page | 30 a line |
59: | `run_llm_calls` | Every model call, one line each, under a header with time in calls, p50/p95 latency, the most calls at once, failures by status and, for models the organizers host, the queue wait | 35 a call |
60: | `run_profile` | Where the time went, per 30 s, 1 min or 5 min: inputs and screen activity per browser, model calls, seconds and cost; then the critical path | 1.5–3k |
61: | `run_screenshot` | A browser's screen at a time with the clicks just before it marked, every browser at once (`browser: "all"`), or a filmstrip (`frames`) | 1.5k an image |
62: | `run_inputs` | The clicks, scrolls and typing the platform recorded in each browser, with their times | 25 an input |
63: | `compare_runs` | Two runs side by side: package, quality, time, cost, cost × time, calls and failures per model, phases, points per field and answer fields that changed | 1–2k |
64: | `wait_for_run` | Wait until a run is running or done, including recording collection and scoring (at most `timeout_s`, default 50 s), then say how it stands | 300 |
65: | `list_submissions` | Your scored submissions: review status, any organizer note, result and package | 60 a submission |
66: | `get_submission` | One submission (`sub_...`): review status, any organizer note, its runs | 300–800 |
67: | `run_package` | The package a run or submission used, as uploaded: SHA-256, label, agent.json and each file's size, never the contents; `out` saves the `.tar.gz` in a folder | 15 a file |
68: | `leaderboard` | The board with each entry's cost × time and the Pareto front, your rank and the gap to the next; `compare_run` places one of your runs on it | 500 |
69: | `models` | The models the organizers host, if any, and how to call them from your computer through `atira models proxy` | 300 |
70: | `test_run` | Pack a folder and start a test run; returns its id, queue place, package SHA-256 and label (the git commit by default) | 150 |
71: | `cancel_run` | Cancel one of your runs that hasn't finished; only with `confirm: true` | 60 |
72: | `submit` | Pack a folder and submit it for a scored run, public and final; only with `confirm: true` after the person said yes | 100 |
73: 
74: Everything only reads, except `test_run`, `cancel_run` and `submit`, and `run_package` with `out`, which saves a file on your computer. A scored submission is public and can't be undone, and a cancelled run
75: doesn't come back, so `submit` and `cancel_run` refuse unless the call says `confirm: true`: tell your agent to ask
76: you first. Your agent sees only what your team sees on the run page; another team's run is "404: run not found".
77: 
78: Run tools take a run id (`run_...`), a test run id (`reh_...`) or a submission id (`sub_...`, meaning its latest run).
79: `run_package` takes the same ids; a submission id there means the package it submitted, which its runs ran.
80: 
81: ## What it shows
82: 
83: `get_run` while a run waits, then once it failed:
84: 
85: ```
86: run_8af0981b3710558a · test run on the public dataset · package 3f2a1c9e0b12 (2 files) "a41c2d9-dirty"
87: Status queued, phase queued
88: Queued: 2 runs ahead of yours, starts in about 3 min
89: ...
90: Status failed, phase done · Failure: Run exited with code 0 without submitting an answer (no answer)
91: ```
92: 
93: `run_llm_calls`:
94: 
95: ```
96: run_0d7f1203b576189a · 86 model calls in a run of 16:22 · $0.4130
97: Time in calls 6:41 · latency p50 2.1s, p95 31s · at most 4 at once (at 02:13)
98:   anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5: 33 calls, $0.4126, 57,619 in (72,128 cached) / 5,867 out, 2:05 in calls
99:   openai/gpt-5-mini: 1 call, $0.0004, 1,845 in / 12 out, 1.2s in calls
100: Failures: openai: 52 failed (429 rate limited)
101: 
102: [02:10.4 +3.2s] anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5 200 in 4,210 (cached 3,900) out 312 $0.00471 id=c_812
103: [02:13.9 +0.4s] openai 429 rate limited $0.00 id=c_815
104: ```
105: 
106: `run_profile` (the screen columns are seconds the browser's screen was changing; `–` is still):
107: 
108: ```
109: time   b1 in · screen  b2 in · screen  b3 in · screen  b4 in · screen  calls  in calls  busy  cost
110: 02:00  6 · 21s         3 · 8.0s        10 · 44s        0 · –           14     1:02      48s   $0.0612
111: 03:00  4 · 12s         0 · –           0 · –           2 · 3.5s        3      41s       38s   $0.0140
112: Critical path:
113: Longest stretches over 10 s with no input, no screen change and no model call in flight:
114:   03:12.4–04:40.1 (01:27)
115:     last line before: [03:11.9] stdout: mail TAN: waiting for the TAN message
116: Browsers that went quiet:
117:   browser 3: last screen change at 02:45.4, then nothing for 04:53 until the end
118: ```
119: 
120: `diagnose_run` names the failure's class and the next step: `cancelled`, `no answer` (your agent system ended
121: without entering one: fix it, a rerun alone won't help), `agent exit` (see stderr), `timeout` (make it faster),
122: `answer rejected` (fix the answer's shape) or `platform` (not your agent system: rerun it as it is). A reason that
123: starts with "Setup" is agent.json's setup: `run_logs` with stream `setup` shows why. Where the platform records a
124: run's failure class, that one is used.
125: 
126: ## Times
127: 
128: Times are on the run's clock, as the run page shows them: `02:13`, `1:02:13`, `3m20s` or `133` seconds from the
129: run's start, or an ISO 8601 time; durations are written the same way. The same time in the run page's address,
130: `?t=02:13`, opens the replay there. Links point at the platform's own address, whichever name the CLI talks to.
131: 
132: A screenshot is cut from the recording with ffmpeg on the platform. If the platform can't do that right now, the
133: CLI cuts it with your own ffmpeg (`brew install ffmpeg`, or `sudo apt install ffmpeg`); without one it says so and
134: links the replay. A time outside a recording gets its nearest frame and says so ("browser 1's recording covers
135: -00:03.7–07:48.9").
136: 
137: ## What it can't do
138: 
139: - **Past frames of a live run.** The recording is stored after the run ends and collection finishes; until then `run_screenshot` shows each
140:   browser's latest live frame, about a second behind the screen (its time says when), and
141:   filmstrips and screen activity wait for the end. The run page's live view shows it moving.
142: - **Logs as they arrive.** Tools answer once; `wait_for_run` waits up to 600 s if your client allows long tool calls
143:   (Codex stops a tool after 60 s unless you raise `tool_timeout_sec`). In a terminal, `atira logs <run> --follow`
144:   streams a run's logs until it ends.
145: - **Log streams** are `setup`, `stdout`, `stderr` and `input`: errors are in `stderr` and in `get_run`/`diagnose_run`,
146:   screen activity is in `run_profile`.
147: - **Typed secrets.** Inputs show typed text with keys, tokens and your run's secrets masked.
148: 
149: From a terminal, `atira cancel <run>` cancels a run and `atira status` lists your submissions and test runs.
150: 
151: ## Try it
152: 
153: Ask your agent things like:
154: 
155: - "Why did my last test run fail? Diagnose it, then show me the screen at the moment it went idle."
156: - "Where did the time go in run_19932ad4ade523e4? Which model calls were slowest?"
157: - "Compare my last two test runs: what changed in the score and the cost?"
158: - "Start a test run of ./my-agent, wait until it's running, and show me every browser's screen at 01:00."
159: - "Which files did my latest submission's package have? Save it to ./downloaded and diff it against ./my-agent."
160: 
161: This guide is at `$API/docs/mcp.md`.
162:

1: # MCP Servers (`mcp_config.json`)
2: 
3: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables developers to
4: build secure, two-way integrations between AI models and their data/tools. In
5: Antigravity, configuring MCP servers allows you to expose custom tools,
6: resources, and prompts to the agent.
7: 
8: MCP servers can be configured globally or packaged within plugins.
9: 
10: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
11: 
12: ## Configuration File (`mcp_config.json`)
13: 
14: MCP servers are defined in a `mcp_config.json` file. The file contains a map of
15: server identifiers to their respective configurations.
16: 
17: ### Location
18: 
19: *   **Global Configuration**: `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` (applies to all
20:     sessions).
21: *   **Plugin Configuration**: `plugins/<plugin_name>/mcp_config.json` (active
22:     when the plugin is enabled).
23: 
24: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
25: 
26: ## Configuration Schema
27: 
28: Antigravity supports two transport mechanisms for MCP: **Stdio** (for local
29: command-line tools) and **SSE** (for remote services).
30: 
31: ```json
32: {
33:   "mcpServers": {
34:     "sqlite-helper": {
35:       "command": "sqlite-mcp-server",
36:       "args": ["/path/to/database.db"],
37:       "env": {
38:         "DB_READONLY": "true"
39:       }
40:     },
41:     "remote-service": {
42:       "serverUrl": "https://mcp.mycompany.com/sse"
43:     }
44:   }
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: ### 1. Stdio Transport (Local)
49: 
50: Used to run a local executable or script as an MCP server. The Language Server
51: spawns the process and communicates with it over standard input/output.
52: 
53: *   **`command`** (string, required): The executable to run (e.g., `node`,
54:     `python3`, or a binary name).
55: *   **`args`** (array of strings, optional): Arguments to pass to the command.
56: *   **`env`** (object, optional): Environment variables to inject into the
57:     server process.
58: 
59: ### 2. SSE Transport (Remote)
60: 
61: Used to connect to a remote MCP server over HTTP using Server-Sent Events (SSE).
62: 
63: *   **`serverUrl`** (string, required): The HTTP(S) URL of the remote MCP
64:     endpoint.
65: 
66: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
67: 
68: ## How the Agent Uses MCP
69: 
70: Once an MCP server is configured and successfully connected:
71: 
72: 1.  **Tool Discovery**: The system queries the server for its available tools.
73: 2.  **Tool Injection**: Discovered tools are automatically added to the agent's
74:     toolset and listed in the system prompt.
75: 3.  **Execution**: When the agent calls an MCP tool, the Language Server routes
76:     the request to the MCP server, executes it, and returns the result to the
77:     agent.
78: 
79: ## Scoping and Scannability
80: 
81: *   **Global Servers**: Active for all conversations.
82: *   **Plugin Servers**: Only active when the parent plugin is loaded. Their
83:     tools are automatically prefixed or namespaced if necessary to avoid
84:     conflicts.
85: *   You can inspect active MCP servers and their tools in the UI by navigating
86:     to **Additional Options (...) > MCP Servers**.
87:
